1205.title: The Niggun: A Song Without Words
1205.hook: the niggun climbs from sadness to joy to stillness
1205.carry: a wordless niggun climbs toward god
1205.tomorrow: The Rebbetzins and the Maiden of Ludmir
1205.howItsDone: Hasidim sing niggunim at the Shabbat table, at a rebbe's gathering, before prayer and at celebrations; a tune is often repeated many times, slowly building and then quieting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why Hasidim dress as they do: the long coat and the fur hat holding a memory of old Eastern Europe, and the gartel tied on for prayer. A new week begins, with a song.
screen: `DRESS THAT REMEMBERS, DRESS TO MEET GOD.`

segments.voice: Yai, dai, bim, bam. What do those syllables mean? Nothing. You won't find them in a dictionary. And yet a group of Hasidim can sing them over and over, slow at first, almost sad. Then the tune picks up. Hands drum on whatever is nearby. Somebody stands. And then, somehow, it slows again, softer and softer, until the singers are only breathing. The song leads them there. Hasidim have a name for that kind of song, and a picture for where it takes you.
screen: `YAI, DAI, BIM, BAM.` → `NO DICTIONARY HAS THEM.` → `THE SONG LEADS.`

segments.voice: A ladder of song. The Hebrew word is niggun, a melody, and in Hasidic life it often means a tune sung without words. First, why no words. Words can only say what they say. Hasidic teachers describe the wordless tune as reaching past language, to a place the heart knows but can't name. A syllable like yai has nothing to argue with. Second, the climb. Some niggunim move in stages. They begin in longing, sometimes close to sadness. They rise into joy. And some end in stillness, a quiet the song has earned. That's the ladder: down where you are, up toward God, and then a rung where even the song stops. In Genesis, Jacob dreams of "a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven." The niggun is a ladder you can sing. Third, an old precedent. In the book of Kings, the prophet Elisha needs to hear God's word, and he asks for music first: "But now bring me a minstrel. And it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the LORD came upon him." Music came before the message. Fourth, how it lives. Courts keep their own niggunim, some said to come from their founding rebbes, and pass them down like the coats from yesterday. Tradition says some Hasidic leaders composed tunes, and some adopted folk melodies they heard around them, believing a holy spark was waiting inside. A shepherd's song could become a prayer.
screen: `A TUNE WITHOUT WORDS.` · `LONGING, JOY, STILLNESS.` · `BRING ME A MINSTREL.` · `A SHEPHERD'S SONG, LIFTED.` · then, large: `A LADDER OF SONG.`

segments.voice: Hum a slow tune, any you know or just a few notes on one syllable like yai or dai, starting low and a little sad if that's where you are. Let it lift on its own, brighter and faster if it wants to, then slow again, softer, until you're only humming on the breath. Stop, and stay in the quiet the tune left behind; if you can't make a sound where you are, hum it inside.
A ladder of song. The niggun, a Hasidic melody often sung without words, that can climb from longing to joy to stillness. Today's word.
Your line: a wordless niggun climbs toward God. On an ordinary evening, it asks only that you hum. See you tomorrow.

1206.title: The Rebbetzins and the Maiden of Ludmir
1206.hook: rebbetzins and women teachers shaped Hasidic life
1206.carry: women, too, taught and held the courts
1206.howItsDone: In Hasidic communities the rebbetzin receives women seeking advice and blessings, leads women's gatherings and organizes much of the court's life; stories of earlier rebbetzins and women teachers are retold in Hasidic homes and books.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the niggun: a wordless tune climbing from longing to joy to stillness. Today, the people in the next room.

In the Hasidic stories on this path so far, the star is usually a rebbe. He sits at the head of the table, he gives the blessing, he tells the parable. But follow the story into the next room. Who decided who got in to see him today? Who sat with the woman whose child was sick, while the men crowded the study hall? Who kept the household of a court running, with guests at every meal? The stories mention these people less often. They were there all along. Today turns the camera.
screen: `THE REBBE AT THE TABLE.` → `FOLLOW THE STORY NEXT DOOR.` → `TURN THE CAMERA.`

segments.voice: Women of the court. First, the rebbetzin. In Yiddish, a rebbe's wife is the rebbetzin. Hasidic tradition remembers rebbetzins who were far more than a wife at the rebbe's side. Women came to them with their troubles and their requests for blessings. They advised, organized and held communities together through hard years. Some were known for their own learning and wisdom, and Hasidim told stories about them, too. Second, the daughters. Hasidic tradition tells of Edel, the daughter of the Baal Shem Tov, as a woman of wisdom and holiness, and her daughter Feiga was the mother of Rebbe Nachman, whom you met this past week. A line of teaching ran through the women of the family as well as the men. Third, a teacher of her own. Tradition tells of Hannah Rachel Verbermacher, called the Maiden of Ludmir. The story says she studied deeply, prayed with intensity, and drew followers who came to hear her teach on Shabbat, a role usually held by men. Her story comes down as tradition, and the tellings differ in their details. But people kept telling it. Fourth, the older picture. The book of Proverbs ends with a portrait of a woman of valor, a passage some Jewish families sing at the Friday night table. One line says: "She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness." That verse fits the women of the courts. In the stories, much of their teaching happens in kitchens and side rooms rather than at the head of the table. It shaped Hasidic life anyway.
screen: `THE REBBETZIN.` · `EDEL AND FEIGA.` · `THE MAIDEN OF LUDMIR.` · `WISDOM AND THE LAW OF KINDNESS.` · then, large: `WOMEN OF THE COURT.`

1207.title: Hasidism for everyone
1207.hook: Buber, Heschel and Zalman Schachter-Shalomi brought Hasidic ideas to wide audiences
1207.howItsDone: Readers meet Hasidic ideas through Buber's retold tales and Heschel's books, and in Jewish Renewal and other communities that sing niggunim and tell Hasidic stories; Hasidic courts continue their own life of study and prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, women of the court: rebbetzins, daughters and teachers who shaped Hasidic life from the side rooms. Today, Hasidism walks out the door.

Rabbi Zusya lies on his deathbed, and he's afraid. His students are puzzled. You, afraid? He answers with a story about himself. When I come before the heavenly court, he says, they won't ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Moses? They'll ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Zusya? That little tale was told among Hasidim. Then it traveled. It turns up in sermons, classrooms and graduation speeches, far from any rebbe's table. Today: how it got there.
screen: `ZUSYA, AFRAID.` → `WHY WEREN'T YOU ZUSYA?` → `THE TALE TRAVELED.`

segments.voice: Hasidism for everyone. Three teachers carried Hasidic ideas beyond the court. First, Martin Buber. He gathered Hasidic tales from old Hebrew and Yiddish books and retold them in German, and from there they reached English. Through him, readers who would never visit a court met Zusya and the Baal Shem Tov. Buber heard in Hasidism a teaching that God is met in the ordinary meeting between people, here, now, not somewhere far away. Second, Abraham Joshua Heschel. He came from a family of Hasidic rebbes and became a teacher and writer in America. In his book on the Sabbath, he describes Shabbat as holiness in time rather than in a place, a sanctuary built of hours. He wrote about wonder, and about a God who cares about human beings. Third, Zalman Schachter-Shalomi, usually called Reb Zalman. He was trained in Chabad, then helped found what became Jewish Renewal, bringing niggunim, Hasidic stories and meditative prayer into new communities. Fourth, the argument. Not everyone was pleased. Some critics, including the scholar Gershom Scholem, said Buber picked out the tales, set aside the Hasidic teachers' own written teachings, and read his own philosophy into what was left. Some Hasidim would say the court, its law and its life, is the point. Others answer that the sparks were always meant to travel. You don't have to settle it. Notice only that Zusya's question now gets asked in rooms where no one wears a shtreimel.
screen: `BUBER RETELLS THE TALES.` · `HESCHEL: HOLINESS IN TIME.` · `REB ZALMAN AND RENEWAL.` · `NOT EVERYONE WAS PLEASED.` · then, large: `HASIDISM BEYOND THE COURT.`

segments.voice: Let Zusya's question come to you in your own name: not why weren't you someone braver or holier or more famous, just why weren't you you? Is there one part of yourself you've been setting aside to look like someone else? Don't scold yourself; just notice it and breathe with it, and if you pray, hold the question there.
Hasidism for everyone. Buber, Heschel and Reb Zalman carried Hasidic tales and ideas to wide audiences, and people still argue about what traveled and what stayed behind. Today's word.
Your line: hasidism beyond the court. A deathbed question can travel a very long way. See you tomorrow.

1208.title: Mussar and Hasidism
1208.hook: Mussar and Hasidism were once rivals; many now learn from both
1208.carry: depart from evil, and do good: both halves
1208.howItsDone: Students of Mussar study short ethical texts daily, keep a cheshbon hanefesh, an evening accounting of the soul, and work on one trait at a time, often with a study partner or group; Hasidim pursue inner growth through prayer, song, joy and a rebbe's teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hasidism beyond the court: Buber, Heschel and Reb Zalman carrying the tales outward, and Zusya asking why he wasn't Zusya. Today, a rival path.

Two people want the same thing: to become better. One keeps a small notebook. Every night she writes down where she lost her temper, where she was stingy, where she told a little lie, and she works on one trait at a time, patiently, for weeks. The other one sings. He dances at the Shabbat table, he looks for God in the bread and the work, and he trusts that joy will carry him upward. Both are serious. Both are Jewish paths. For a long time, their followers eyed each other across the room.

Two paths inward. First, the word mussar. In the book of Proverbs it means instruction, discipline: "My son, hear the instruction of thy father." The Mussar movement took that word as its name. It grew among Lithuanian Jews around Rabbi Israel Salanter and his students, and later took root in the yeshivas. Its tools are plain: study a little ethical teaching every day, take an honest accounting of the soul, called cheshbon hanefesh, and work on your traits, your middot, one at a time. Second, the Hasidic path, which you've walked this whole block: joy, clinging to God, service through ordinary life, the rebbe and the song. Third, the rivalry. These grew up in different worlds. The Lithuanian yeshivas came out of communities that had opposed Hasidism, and each side could find the other too cold or too loose, too gloomy or too carefree. One way people describe the difference uses a single verse from the Psalms: "Depart from evil, and do good." Mussar tends to start with the first half, facing your faults squarely. Hasidism tends to start with the second, doing good and letting the darkness fall away. Fourth, today. The old lines have softened. Some teachers now draw on both: the notebook and the song, the honest accounting and the joy. Heard together, they sound less like rivals and more like two halves of the same verse. Neither one has to win for you to learn from either.

Then try the song: remember one good thing you did recently, however small, and let yourself be glad of it. Feel the difference between the two, then just breathe with both.
Two paths inward. Mussar's honest accounting and work on character, and Hasidism's joy and closeness to God: once rivals, now learned side by side by some. Today's word.
Your line: depart from evil, and do good: both halves. Mussar's notebook and Hasidism's song can share one table. Rest well.

1209.title: If Not Higher
1209.hook: the mystical path ends in ordinary kindness
1209.carry: the mystic's climb ends in quiet kindness
1209.howItsDone: Jews practice gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness, by visiting the sick, feeding guests, helping the poor and caring for the dead; Hasidic and kabbalistic teachers count such acts as part of the spiritual path, not apart from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mussar and Hasidism: the notebook and the song, two halves of one verse. Today, a rebbe goes missing.
screen: `DEPART FROM EVIL, AND DO GOOD: BOTH HALVES.`

segments.voice: Before dawn, in the days of penitential prayers before the High Holidays, the rebbe of Nemirov vanishes. His Hasidim say he goes up to heaven to plead for them. A skeptical visitor doesn't buy it. One night he hides under the rebbe's bed to see for himself. Before light, the rebbe gets up, puts on rough peasant clothes, takes an axe and walks out of town into the woods. The visitor follows, heart pounding. What does a mystic do in the dark, alone, with an axe?
screen: `THE REBBE VANISHES.` → `A SKEPTIC UNDER THE BED.` → `AN AXE IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Mystic kindness. The story comes from the Yiddish writer I. L. Peretz, and it's called "If Not Higher." First, the ending. The rebbe chops wood, ties it in a bundle and carries it to a broken-down hut where a sick widow lies alone. He tells her he's a peasant selling wood, and when she says she can't pay, he says he'll trust her. He lights her stove himself, saying the penitential prayers under his breath as he works. The skeptic watches it all. After that, whenever the Hasidim say their rebbe goes up to heaven, the visitor adds quietly: if not higher. Second, the path you've walked. This whole block has climbed: ten lights, broken vessels and scattered sparks, cleaving to God, a ladder of song. And here the climb comes down to a stove and a bundle of wood. The story suggests this is where the ladder was leading all along. Third, the old teaching underneath. The sages of Pirkei Avot say the world stands on three things: Torah, worship and acts of loving-kindness. And the prophet Micah asks: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Fourth, why the disguise. The rebbe hides who he is so the widow keeps her dignity. Kindness here is quiet, unseen, and costs him his sleep. No one in the town knows, except a skeptic hiding under the bed. That's the mystic's secret in this story: the highest place may be a widow's cold hut before dawn.
screen: `WOOD FOR A SICK WIDOW.` · `THE CLIMB COMES DOWN.` · `TORAH, WORSHIP, KINDNESS.` · `KINDNESS IN DISGUISE.` · then, large: `MYSTIC KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who could use a little warmth: a neighbor, a coworker, someone at home, someone alone. Ask what would actually help them, a meal, a call, a ride, carrying something heavy, rather than what would look good. Then picture a way to do it quietly, so it keeps their dignity and doesn't need your name on it.
Mystic kindness. The teaching, told in Peretz's rebbe of Nemirov, that the mystical climb comes down to an ordinary, quiet act of care. Today's word.
Your line: the mystic's climb ends in quiet kindness. The rebbe of Nemirov went up, if not higher, to a widow's cold stove. I'll be here tomorrow.

1210.title: Block close: the hidden light (Chagigah 12a)
1210.hook: the light of creation was hidden away for the righteous
1210.howItsDone: Jews read the creation story aloud in synagogue when the Torah reading cycle begins again, and the Talmud's teaching on the hidden light is studied in Chagigah and retold in kabbalistic and Hasidic teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mystic kindness: the rebbe of Nemirov in peasant clothes, lighting a sick widow's stove before dawn. If not higher.

"And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." That's the first day of creation. Keep reading Genesis and you reach the fourth day, when God makes the sun, the moon and the stars. So a careful reader stops: if the sun came on day four, what was the light of day one? The rabbis of the Talmud asked exactly that. Their answer closes this whole block on Kabbalah and Hasidic thought, because it's a story about light that's still here, just out of sight.

segments.voice: The hidden light. First, the passage. In the Talmud, tractate Chagigah, the sages teach that the light of the first day was a different light. By it, the first human being could see from one end of the world to the other. But when God foresaw generations who would misuse it, God hid it away, set aside for the righteous in the time to come. Second, a verse that keeps it close. The Psalm says: "Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart." Sown, like a seed: hidden, but planted, waiting to come up. Third, where the light went. Teachings handed down in the Baal Shem Tov's name say the hidden light was tucked into the Torah itself, so whoever studies it with love can catch a glimmer now. That's the whole block in one picture. You began with the received, and a warning to enter carefully. Letters that create, ten lights, broken vessels, a shard to repair. Then the Hasidim: no place without him, cling, joy opens, less me, two souls, truth, fiercely, hidden will, a ladder of song, mystic kindness. Fourth, the thread running through them. Again and again, these teachings say the light didn't leave. It's hidden, scattered, sown, waiting in a page, a song, a stove before dawn. Next comes a new block: the movements of modern Jewish life, side by side, without ranking.
screen: `THE LIGHT OF THE FIRST DAY.` · `LIGHT IS SOWN FOR THE RIGHTEOUS.` · `TUCKED INTO THE TORAH.` · `THE LIGHT DIDN'T LEAVE.` · then, large: `THE HIDDEN LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Think back across the last few weeks and find one moment when something good showed up where you didn't expect it: a kind word, a song, a person who stayed. Let it brighten in your mind for a few breaths. Then rest your gaze on one ordinary thing near you, a cup, a window, a hand, and let it be enough just to look.
Block close. The hidden light of Chagigah: the light of the first day, put away for the righteous, which Hasidic teachers find sown in the Torah and in ordinary life. Today's word.
Your line: the hidden light. Hidden isn't gone; it's sown. One block closes, and another opens tomorrow.

1211.title: The Movements of Jewish Life
1211.hook: modern Jews organize themselves in movements; no single one speaks for all
1211.carry: these and these: no stream speaks for all
1211.howItsDone: Jews may belong to a synagogue affiliated with a movement, such as Orthodox, Conservative or Masorti, Reform, Reconstructionist or Renewal, or to an independent or Sephardi community, or to none; each movement has its own seminaries, prayer books and understanding of Jewish law.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the block on Kabbalah and Hasidism with the hidden light: the first day's light, put away and sown for the righteous. Today, a new block.

Three Jewish friends walk into a coffee shop on a Saturday morning. Well, two of them do. The third is at synagogue, and won't use his phone until Shabbat ends, so the group chat will have to wait. One of the two in the coffee shop is heading to her own synagogue later, where the prayers mix Hebrew and English. The other one lights candles on Friday night and calls herself just Jewish, no label. All three are telling the truth. Today is the map that shows all three at once.
screen: `SATURDAY MORNING, A COFFEE SHOP.` → `ONE AT SYNAGOGUE, PHONE OFF.` → `ALL THREE TELLING THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Many streams. Back on day nine hundred seventy-five, you watched Reform begin. Now, the whole map. In modern Hebrew, the movements are often called zeramim, streams. First, the names. Orthodox Judaism, which itself holds many communities, from Modern Orthodox to Haredi, including the Hasidic courts you just met. Conservative Judaism, called Masorti in Israel and elsewhere. Reform Judaism. Reconstructionist Judaism. And others, like Jewish Renewal, which Reb Zalman helped begin. Second, what divides them: how Jewish law binds today, who has the authority to decide, and how tradition meets modern life. They answer differently, and sometimes they disagree sharply about each other. Third, what the map leaves out. Some Sephardi and Mizrahi communities don't sort neatly into these labels. Some Jews belong to no movement at all, and some move between them over a lifetime. A label tells you something about a synagogue. It tells you less about a person. Fourth, the old argument. The Talmud tells of the schools of Hillel and Shammai, who argued for years until a voice from heaven said: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows Hillel. Some people today reach for that line to describe the movements. Others say it was about two schools inside one law and doesn't stretch that far. That disagreement is part of the map too. And the rule for this whole block: no single movement speaks for all Jews, and this path won't rank them. The Psalm has a picture for it: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God."
screen: `ORTHODOX, CONSERVATIVE, REFORM …` · `HOW DOES THE LAW BIND?` · `A LABEL TELLS YOU LESS.` · `THESE AND THESE.` · then, large: `MANY STREAMS.`
